what_its_for: Cefadroxil is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections such as throat infections (strep throat), skin infections, and urinary tract infections (UTIs). It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It does NOT work for viral infections like colds or the flu.
how_to_take: Take cefadroxil by mouth with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Swallow capsules or tablets whole. If you have a liquid (suspension), shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with a proper measuring spoon or oral syringe — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Always finish your entire course of antibiotics, even if you start feeling better. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back and make the antibiotic less effective in the future.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your infection, age, and kidney function. Common adult doses range from 500 mg to 1,000 mg (1 gram) taken once or twice a day. Children's doses are based on body weight. Always follow the exact dose and schedule your doctor prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store capsules and tablets at room temperature (59°F to 77°F / 15°C to 25°C) in a cool, dry place away from heat, moisture, and light. Keep the liquid suspension in the refrigerator — do NOT freeze it. Throw away any unused liquid after 14 days. Keep all medication out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking cefadroxil if you are allergic to penicillin or other cephalosporin antibiotics without first talking to your doctor, as you may have a cross-allergy. Do not skip doses or stop taking the medication early, even if you feel better. Avoid drinking alcohol excessively while on antibiotics, as it can weaken your immune system and slow recovery. Tell your doctor before taking antacids or supplements containing calcium, magnesium, or aluminum, as these can sometimes affect how antibiotics work.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency care right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (hives, rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, or dizziness); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody, which could be a sign of a serious gut infection called C. difficile; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine or unusual tiredness; seizures; or if your infection does not improve or gets worse after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting cefadroxil. However, it is very important to keep taking the full course of antibiotics as prescribed, even when you feel better. The full course typically lasts 7 to 14 days depending on your infection. If you do not feel any improvement after 3 days, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease or reduced kidney function, your doctor may lower your dose or have you take it less often. Be sure to tell your doctor about any kidney problems. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Cefadroxil is generally considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding so they can weigh the benefits and risks for you. Elderly patients: Older adults may need a lower dose if their kidneys do not work as well. Children: Cefadroxil is safe for use in children, with doses adjusted based on body weight. The liquid form is available for younger children who cannot swallow capsules.
